source_messages.text: I'm starting a tiny document-outline utility. Everything lives in one module; each function takes a single JSON-style argument and returns a JSON-style value. The first piece, parse_heading, already works: it recognizes markdown heading lines (one to six '#' characters followed by one space) and returns the level plus the raw title text after that first space — it deliberately does not trim anything. Anything else gets None. Two standing decisions for everything we build here: (1) Titles stored in outlines, and therefore anything derived from them, must be stripped of surrounding whitespace. (2) Documents are messy — any line that is not a well-formed heading (plain prose, '#' with no following space, more than six '#', or a heading whose title is blank once stripped) is just content. Skip it quietly; never fail the whole parse over such a line.

request.text: Implement build_outline(lines). lines must be a list of strings; if it is not a list, or any element is not a string, return exactly {"error": "invalid input"}. Use parse_heading to recognize heading lines — don't re-implement that detection. Following the standing decisions, silently ignore every non-heading line and every heading whose title is empty once stripped, and store each node's title stripped of surrounding whitespace. Return the top-level nodes as a list in document order, each node shaped {"title": ..., "level": ..., "children": [...]}. Nesting rule: a heading becomes a child of the most recent heading with a strictly lower level; if there is no such heading, it is top-level. An empty input list yields [].

source_messages.text: The outline builder is in. Two things before we move on. First, a forward-looking note: when we add the lookup tool later, I want query matching to ignore letter case — 'intro' should find 'Intro'. Second, the section index. It should run straight off the raw document lines: it builds the outline itself by calling build_outline, then walks the resulting outline depth-first (a parent, then its children, then the next sibling) and numbers sections. Top-level headings are "1", "2", and so on; children extend the parent's number with their position among the siblings, joined with dots at every depth. To pin the numbering down: numbers always follow a heading's original position among its siblings, counted before anything is left out — so if a heading ends up excluded, later siblings keep the numbers they already had rather than sliding up, and the sequence can skip. One scope-limited policy: only headings of level 3 or less get index entries — level 4 and deeper, along with everything beneath them, are left out of the index entirely. That cutoff belongs to indexing only.

request.text: Implement index_sections(lines). lines is the same list-of-strings document that build_outline accepts. Get the outline by calling build_outline(lines) — reuse it; do not re-implement heading detection, stripping, or nesting — and if it returns its error object, pass that object through unchanged as your result. From that outline, return a list of entries in depth-first pre-order (a parent, then its children, then the next sibling), one entry {"number": ..., "title": ...} per included heading. Numbering: a heading's number chain uses its original 1-based position among its siblings, joined with dots at every depth (top-level headings are "1", "2", ...; the children of section "1" are "1.1", "1.2", ...). Positions are counted before any exclusion: a heading that receives no entry still consumes its sibling position, so later siblings keep their original numbers and the sequence may skip. Per the indexing cutoff, include only headings whose level is 1, 2 or 3; skip any deeper node together with its whole subtree. An empty line list yields an empty outline and therefore [].

source_messages.text: Last piece now: the lookup. One correction to what I told you before — scrap the case-insensitive plan for queries. Matching must be case-sensitive after all: 'intro' must not match 'Intro'; only identical letter case counts.

request.text: Implement query_sections(request). request must be an object containing "lines" (the document line list accepted by build_outline) and "text" (the query string). If request is not an object, or either key is missing, or text is not a non-empty string, return exactly {"error": "invalid query"}. Get the section index by calling index_sections(lines) — reuse it; do not re-implement the build or the numbering — and if it returns its error object, pass that object through unchanged as your result. A section matches when the query text occurs somewhere in its title with exactly matching letter case, per the corrected rule from my last message. Return {"matches": [...]} where each match is {"number": ..., "title": ...} in index order; when nothing matches, return {"matches": []}.

rounds.reference_patch:
def index_sections(lines):
    outline = build_outline(lines)
    if isinstance(outline, dict):
        return outline
    entries = []
    stack = []
    position = len(outline) - 1
    while position >= 0:
        stack.append((outline[position], str(position + 1)))
        position -= 1
    while stack:
        node, number = stack.pop()
        level = node["level"]
        if level > 3:
            continue
        entries.append({"number": number, "title": node["title"]})
        children = node["children"]
        child_pos = len(children) - 1
        while child_pos >= 0:
            stack.append((children[child_pos], number + "." + str(child_pos + 1)))
            child_pos -= 1
    return entries

source_messages.text: Conventions for this project: every function takes exactly one JSON-style argument and returns JSON-compatible values. Any input that does not meet its specification is rejected by returning exactly the string "invalid" (no exceptions, no other sentinel). A sample entry is an object with required keys "id" (a non-empty string), "conc" (a number strictly greater than 0) and "vol" (a number strictly greater than 0); it may also carry "flag" (a boolean, default false) and "group" (a non-empty string, default "unassigned"). Booleans are not numbers here. The existing clean_sample helper is the single place where entries are validated and normalized; whenever later functions need sample data they must call clean_sample rather than re-checking the fields themselves. Extra keys on any object are permitted and are simply ignored.

request.text: Implement normalize_batch. Its argument must be an object with "samples" (a non-empty list of sample entries) and "dilution" (a number strictly greater than 0); if that shape does not hold, return "invalid". Validate every entry by calling clean_sample; if any entry is rejected, return "invalid". Otherwise return an object {"samples": [...], "total_mass": number}. For each entry, in the same order as the input list, emit {"id", "adj_conc", "mass", "flag", "group"} where adj_conc is the cleaned concentration multiplied by the dilution and mass is adj_conc multiplied by the cleaned volume, carrying the cleaned flag and group values through. total_mass is the sum of all mass values. Use ordinary floating point; do not round, format, sort or reorder anything.

source_messages.text: For the aggregation step: flagged samples distort group statistics, so by default an aggregate must leave them out. The caller may pass "include_flagged": true to include everything; any non-boolean value for that key is invalid input. Groups come out sorted alphabetically by group name. Compute everything from normalize_batch output - call it, never duplicate the normalization math yourself.

One thing for later: when we build the final report feature it will present exactly these aggregate numbers, so reports will also exclude flagged samples by default. Keep aggregate_run's interface stable for that.

request.text: Implement aggregate_run. Argument: an object with "samples" (non-empty list of entries), "dilution" (number > 0) and optionally "include_flagged" (boolean, default false). Anything missing, mistyped or rejected downstream returns "invalid". Get the normalized data by calling normalize_batch with the given samples and dilution. Skip flagged samples unless include_flagged is true. Group the remaining samples by their group value and return {"groups": [...], "count": n} where count is the number of samples that went into groups. Each group entry is {"group", "count", "total_mass", "mean_conc"}: the number of samples in that group, the sum of their mass values, and the arithmetic mean of their adj_conc values. Sort the group list by group name ascending. If every sample is filtered out, groups is an empty list and count is 0. No rounding or formatting.

source_messages.text: Update to what I said earlier about the report: the final report is our complete measurement record, so its aggregate section must include flagged samples. When the report aggregates, it should ask for flagged samples to be included. This changes only the report feature - direct aggregate_run calls keep excluding flagged samples unless the caller opts in.

request.text: Implement build_report. Argument: an object with "title" (a non-empty string), "samples" and "dilution" as before; malformed input or any downstream rejection returns "invalid". Build the aggregate section by calling aggregate_run with the given samples and dilution and with include_flagged set to true, per the rule change. Return {"title", "group_count", "grand_total_mass", "top_group", "groups"}: group_count is the number of groups, grand_total_mass is the sum of the groups' total_mass values, groups is exactly the group list aggregate_run produced (same order), and top_group is the name of the group with the largest total_mass; if several tie, report the alphabetically first. Since every sample is included, there is always at least one group. No rounding or reformatting.

source_messages.text: We are building a small pure-Python inventory movement utility. One movement is a JSON object with exactly the fields item, qty and kind. A working parse_movement helper already validates a single entry; treat its behavior as fixed and reuse it rather than revalidating entries by hand.
Understood. I will reuse parse_movement for movement validation and keep its exact behavior.

First feature: batch summarization. Rules: every valid movement contributes to its item's in and out totals, an item's net is in minus out, and the same item appearing in several entries must be merged into one line. The report also carries overall total_in, total_out and the number of movement entries. If any entry is invalid, reject the whole batch and the error must say which zero-based index failed and include the helper's reason; a batch that is not a list is rejected outright with its own message.

request.text: Implement summarize_movements(batch). Exactly: if batch is not a list, return {"ok": false, "error": "batch must be a list"}. Otherwise validate each entry with parse_movement; on the first invalid entry return {"ok": false, "error": "invalid movement at index N: <parse error>"} where N is the entry's zero-based index and <parse error> is the helper's error text. When every entry is valid return {"ok": true, "items": {<item name>: {"in": total_in_for_item, "out": total_out_for_item, "net": in_minus_out}}, "total_in": <sum of all in quantities>, "total_out": <sum of all out quantities>, "count": <number of movement entries>}. An empty batch returns ok with empty items, zero totals and count 0. You may use any loop or comprehension style.

source_messages.text: Next feature: reconcile stock against an opening balance. The payload has opening (item name to nonnegative integer stock), movements (a batch like before), and optionally allow_backorder listing item names allowed to close below zero. Closing balance is opening plus the net movement per item; items that only appear in movements start from zero, and opening items without movement keep their balance.
So closing equals opening plus per-item net. What should happen when a closing balance would drop below zero?

A negative closing balance is rejected unless the item is listed in allow_backorder. If several items violate, name the alphabetically first one together with its balance. Reuse the batch summarizer for movement validation and per-item nets instead of duplicating that logic. One settled directive for later work: an audit feature will be built on top of this, and its policy is already decided - the audit must reject every negative closing balance outright, ignoring any allow_backorder list. That audit directive is scoped to the future audit feature only; reconcile_stock itself keeps the backorder exemption described above.

request.text: Implement reconcile_stock(payload). Exactly: payload must be an object whose only allowed fields are opening, movements and the optional allow_backorder; a non-object payload, a missing opening or movements, or any extra field returns {"ok": false, "error": "payload must contain opening, movements and optional allow_backorder only"}. opening must map nonblank item names (each a string containing at least one non-whitespace character) to nonnegative integers (true/false are not integers), otherwise return {"ok": false, "error": "opening must map item names to nonnegative integers"}. If present, allow_backorder must be a list of nonblank item-name strings (each containing at least one non-whitespace character), otherwise return {"ok": false, "error": "allow_backorder must be a list of item names"}. Then obtain movement validation and per-item nets by calling summarize_movements(payload["movements"]); if that result is not ok, return it unchanged. Compute closing = opening balance plus the item's net, items that only move start from 0, opening-only items keep their balance. If any item not listed in allow_backorder closes below zero, return {"ok": false, "error": "negative closing balance", "item": <alphabetically first such item>, "balance": <its closing value>}. Otherwise return {"ok": true, "closing": {<item>: <closing balance> for every opening or moved item}, "total_in": <from the summary>, "total_out": <from the summary>}.

source_messages.text: About the audit directive I settled earlier - that the audit must reject every negative closing outright, ignoring allow_backorder: scrap it. The audit must follow the same backorder policy as reconciliation - items listed in allow_backorder may close negative and are then reported as shortages, while any other negative closing balance is still rejected.
Acknowledged: the audit follows the reconciliation backorder policy and flags backordered negative items as shortages.

The audit must physically call reconcile_stock with the caller's payload, so any allow_backorder list flows through untouched, and a reconciliation failure must come back unchanged so callers see the exact same error.

request.text: Implement audit_inventory(payload). The payload shape and the negative-balance policy are exactly the current reconcile_stock contract, including the optional allow_backorder list; the earlier audit directive that the audit rejects every negative closing is withdrawn. audit_inventory must call reconcile_stock(payload) and, when that result is not ok, return it unchanged. When reconciliation succeeds, let shortages be the alphabetically sorted list of items whose closing balance is below zero, shortage_count its length, and status the string "clear" when there are no shortages else "shortage". Return {"ok": true, "closing": <the same closing object>, "shortages": [...], "shortage_count": <n>, "status": <"clear" or "shortage">, "total_in": <from the reconciliation result>, "total_out": <from the reconciliation result>}. Do not recompute movement totals yourself; take them from the reconciliation result.

source_messages.text: Project setup for our route utility. The module route_segments.py already has normalize_segment, which returns a canonical segment dict (mode kept, codes uppercased, minutes and fare_cents as integers) or None for anything invalid. Next feature: price_segment(segment), one synchronous positional argument. Validate only via normalize_segment: call it and return None whenever it returns None; never duplicate its checks. If the segment is valid, compute raw = fare_cents + base + rate*minutes, where base is 0 for walk, 140 for bus, 320 for rail, and rate per minute is 0 for walk, 12 for bus, 25 for rail. If minutes is at least 60, apply a 10 percent discount to raw. Standing rule for the whole project: any fractional-cent money result rounds to the nearest whole cent, and an exact half-cent always rounds up. Return a dict with exactly the keys mode, origin, dest, minutes and quote_cents, taking the first four from the normalized segment.

Understood: price_segment will delegate validation to normalize_segment, use the walk/bus/rail base-and-rate table, apply the 10 percent discount at 60 minutes or more with half-up-to-whole-cent rounding, and return the five-field quote dict, or None for invalid input.

request.text: Implement price_segment in route_segments.py now (task price-quote), exactly as specified above.

source_messages.text: Next feature: combine_segments(segments), one synchronous positional argument. The input is a list of segment dicts. If it is not a list or is empty, return None. Normalize each element with the existing normalize_segment (reuse it, do not re-check anything yourself); if any element normalizes to None, return None for the whole call. Then merge adjacent legs: two neighboring legs merge only when they share the same mode AND the first leg's dest equals the second leg's origin; the merged leg keeps that shared mode and the first leg's origin, takes the second leg's dest, and minutes and fare_cents are the sums. Merging chains along a run of mergeable legs and never reorders anything. Output exactly: a dict with key legs (the merged leg dicts with mode, origin, dest, minutes, fare_cents, in original order), key leg_count, key total_minutes (sum of all leg minutes) and key total_fare_cents (sum of all leg fares). One project-wide rule: merging never crosses modes, not here and not in anything built later.

Got it: combine_segments will normalize each element through normalize_segment, merge only adjacent same-mode legs whose endpoints connect, chain runs in order, and report legs, leg_count, total_minutes and total_fare_cents, with None for malformed input or any invalid element.

source_messages.text: Change of plan to one earlier blanket rule: merging-never-crosses-modes is now scoped. combine_segments keeps exactly its current same-mode-only behavior, but the new build_itinerary feature merges further. build_itinerary(request), one synchronous positional argument: request must be a dict with exactly the keys traveler and segments, traveler must be a nonempty string that is not all whitespace; anything else malformed returns None. Run combine_segments on segments; if it returns None, return None. Then fold the combined legs again: whenever a leg's origin equals the previous accumulated leg's dest, merge them, even across modes. The merged leg keeps the earlier leg's mode and origin, takes the later leg's dest, sums fare_cents, and minutes are summed plus a flat 7 transfer minutes whenever the two merged legs have different modes. Finally quote every resulting leg with the existing price_segment and sum the quote_cents; if any quote is None, return None. Output exactly a dict with keys traveler (as given), leg_count, legs (final leg dicts), total_minutes (sum of final leg minutes) and quote_cents (summed quotes).

Clear: build_itinerary will validate the traveler/segments envelope, reuse combine_segments and then price_segment, additionally merge connected legs across modes with a 7 minute transfer penalty while keeping the earlier mode, and return traveler, leg_count, legs, total_minutes and quote_cents, or None on any failure.
